difficultyReason: Short two-speaker dialogue with sharply opposed positions on one central claim. Martina says home cooking is healthier than restaurant food; Reggie explicitly denies this. Four distractors are off-topic or only one speaker addresses them.
stimulus: Martina: People who cook most of their meals at home eat healthier food than people who eat out often. Home cooks control the amount of salt, oil, and sugar in their meals, and restaurant kitchens almost always use more of each than a home cook would. Reggie: That's a myth. Restaurants now publish nutrition information and many of them prepare meals with less salt and oil than the average home cook does. People who eat out regularly are not eating less healthily than those who cook at home.
questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Martina and Reggie are committed to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: restaurants are required by law to publish nutrition information

choices.label: B
choices.text: people who cook at home eat more healthily than people who eat out often

choices.label: C
choices.text: eating too much salt is unhealthy

choices.label: D
choices.text: home cooks enjoy preparing their own meals

choices.label: E
choices.text: restaurants charge more for healthy meals than for unhealthy ones

explanations.correct: Martina asserts that home cooks eat healthier than people who eat out often; Reggie explicitly denies it. That is exactly the proposition at issue.
explanations.A: Neither speaker addresses whether the disclosure is legally required.
explanations.C: Both would agree that excess salt is unhealthy; no disagreement there.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses enjoyment of cooking.

difficultyReason: Direct disagreement about whether a specific policy should be adopted. Speakers use the same vocabulary and contradict each other on the central proposal; distractors are out-of-scope or mutual-agreement traps.
stimulus: Councilor Dent: Our city should ban gasoline-powered leaf blowers. They produce more pollution per hour of use than most cars, and the noise is a nuisance to every neighbor within two blocks. Councilor Vu: A ban is the wrong response. Electric leaf blowers are already widely available, and landscapers are switching to them on their own. The city should not outlaw a tool that is already being phased out voluntarily.
questionStem: Dent and Vu disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: gasoline-powered leaf blowers produce more pollution per hour than most cars

choices.label: B
choices.text: electric leaf blowers are quieter than gasoline-powered ones

choices.label: C
choices.text: the city should prohibit gasoline-powered leaf blowers

choices.label: D
choices.text: landscapers should be free to choose their own equipment

choices.label: E
choices.text: noise from leaf blowers bothers neighbors

explanations.correct: Dent says the city should ban them; Vu says a ban is the wrong response. That is a direct contradiction about the policy.
explanations.A: Dent asserts this claim; Vu does not address it, so their disagreement cannot be established.
explanations.B: Neither speaker compares the noise of electric and gas blowers directly.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a general position on landscaper autonomy.
explanations.E: Dent says neighbors are bothered; Vu does not deny this.

difficultyReason: Two historians dispute a factual claim about cause. One says the invention of the printing press was the primary driver of rising literacy; the other flatly denies it and assigns primacy to schooling. Distractors are off-topic or agreed-upon.
stimulus: Alenka: The rise in European literacy rates between 1500 and 1800 was driven primarily by the printing press. Once books became cheap and abundant, ordinary people had both the opportunity and the incentive to learn to read. Bertil: The printing press mattered, but it was not the primary driver. Literacy rates rose mainly because governments and churches invested in schools that taught children to read. Without that schooling, cheap books would have sat unread.
questionStem: Alenka and Bertil disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: books became cheaper after the printing press was invented

choices.label: B
choices.text: the printing press had any effect on European literacy rates

choices.label: C
choices.text: the printing press was the primary cause of rising literacy in Europe from 1500 to 1800

choices.label: D
choices.text: governments funded schools during the early modern period

choices.label: E
choices.text: literacy rates in Europe rose between 1500 and 1800

explanations.correct: Alenka says the press was primarily responsible; Bertil explicitly denies that it was primary and assigns primacy to schools.
explanations.A: Both would accept that books became cheaper.
explanations.B: Bertil concedes the press 'mattered'; he doesn't deny any effect.
explanations.D: Bertil asserts it; Alenka does not deny it.
explanations.E: Both speakers accept that literacy rates rose.

difficultyReason: Ethics-domain disagreement about a single evaluative claim: whether it is morally permissible to eat animals. Speakers take opposite positions in plain language; distractors are agreement or out-of-scope.
stimulus: Parisa: It is morally wrong to eat animals. Animals can suffer, and we now have abundant, nutritious plant foods available. Causing suffering to a sentient creature when we have good alternatives cannot be justified. Quentin: It is not morally wrong. Humans evolved as omnivores, and raising and eating animals in humane conditions is a long-standing and legitimate practice. Causing some harm is acceptable when the practice serves a genuine human interest.
questionStem: Parisa and Quentin disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: animals are capable of suffering

choices.label: B
choices.text: plant-based foods are nutritionally adequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: humans evolved as omnivores

choices.label: D
choices.text: eating animals is morally wrong

choices.label: E
choices.text: factory farming is humane

explanations.correct: Parisa says it is morally wrong; Quentin says it is not. Direct contradiction of the central claim.
explanations.A: Parisa asserts it; Quentin does not deny it — he accepts that some harm is caused.
explanations.B: Parisa asserts it; Quentin says nothing about plant nutrition.
explanations.C: Quentin asserts it; Parisa does not deny it.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses factory farming specifically.

difficultyReason: Environmental-science dispute where each speaker makes one explicit central claim about wind power's sufficiency. Direct contradiction; distractors are out-of-scope technical points.
stimulus: Sunita: Wind power alone could supply all of our country's electricity needs. Studies estimate that the wind resources across our plains and coastlines could generate several times our current total demand if fully developed. Tomas: Wind cannot supply all of our electricity. The wind does not blow reliably everywhere at once, and without enormous advances in storage we will always need some other source to fill the gaps.
questionStem: Sunita and Tomas disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the country's plains and coastlines have significant wind resources

choices.label: B
choices.text: wind power can supply all of the country's electricity needs

choices.label: C
choices.text: battery storage technology has improved in recent years

choices.label: D
choices.text: wind turbines are a form of renewable energy

choices.label: E
choices.text: electricity demand is growing in the country

explanations.correct: Sunita asserts wind alone could supply all electricity needs; Tomas explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Sunita asserts this; Tomas does not deny it.
explanations.C: Neither speaker addresses recent storage improvements specifically.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the classification of wind as renewable.

difficultyReason: Linguistics domain with a crisp prescriptive versus descriptive disagreement. Speakers contradict each other over one explicit claim about whether 'literally' should be used non-literally.
stimulus: Professor Holm: Using the word 'literally' to mean 'figuratively,' as in 'I literally died laughing,' is simply incorrect. 'Literally' means 'in a literal sense,' and using it to mean the opposite undermines the distinction the word exists to mark. Professor Iyer: That use is not incorrect. Words change meaning through ordinary use, and 'literally' as an intensifier is now so widespread and well understood that it is a legitimate sense of the word.
questionStem: Holm and Iyer disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the non-literal use of 'literally' is widespread

choices.label: B
choices.text: words can change meaning over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: using 'literally' to mean 'figuratively' is incorrect

choices.label: D
choices.text: 'literally' has a literal sense

choices.label: E
choices.text: listeners are usually confused by the non-literal use of 'literally'

explanations.correct: Holm says the use is simply incorrect; Iyer says it is not incorrect. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Iyer asserts it; Holm does not deny that it is widespread.
explanations.B: Iyer asserts it; Holm does not deny it in general.
explanations.D: Both speakers accept that 'literally' has a literal sense.

difficultyReason: Legal-domain dispute with one clear evaluative claim on each side. Speakers directly contradict each other about whether jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials. Distractors are mutual-agreement or off-topic.
stimulus: Wren: Jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials. A jury of twelve ordinary citizens brings a broader range of perspectives than any single judge and is harder for a skilled attorney to manipulate. Xavier: Jury trials are not fairer. Juries are swayed by emotional appeals and often do not understand complex evidence. A seasoned judge is more likely to reach a fair verdict in difficult cases.
questionStem: Wren and Xavier disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials

choices.label: B
choices.text: jurors are ordinary citizens

choices.label: C
choices.text: complex evidence is sometimes presented at trial

choices.label: D
choices.text: attorneys are sometimes skilled at persuasion

choices.label: E
choices.text: judges are appointed rather than elected

explanations.correct: Wren claims jury trials are fairer than bench trials; Xavier explicitly denies that claim. Direct contradiction.
explanations.B: Both accept that jurors are ordinary citizens.
explanations.C: Xavier implies it; Wren does not deny it.
explanations.D: Wren asserts it; Xavier does not deny it.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses how judges are selected.

difficultyReason: Technology domain. Clear disagreement on one factual claim: whether social media has, on balance, worsened teen mental health. Distractors are agreement traps or single-speaker claims.
stimulus: Ori: Widespread social media use has, on balance, worsened teenage mental health over the past fifteen years. Rates of anxiety and depression among teens began climbing at precisely the time smartphones and social platforms became ubiquitous, and many clinicians report a clear link. Petra: Teen mental health has not been worsened by social media on balance. The rise in diagnoses largely reflects greater awareness and willingness to seek treatment, not a real increase in underlying problems caused by these platforms.
questionStem: Ori and Petra disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: smartphones have become ubiquitous among teenagers

choices.label: B
choices.text: social media use has worsened teen mental health on balance

choices.label: C
choices.text: teens should be restricted from using social media

choices.label: D
choices.text: rates of diagnosis for anxiety and depression have risen among teens

choices.label: E
choices.text: clinicians treat teenagers for anxiety and depression

explanations.correct: Ori asserts social media has worsened teen mental health on balance; Petra explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Both accept that smartphones became ubiquitous.
explanations.C: Neither speaker takes a position on restricting use.
explanations.D: Both accept diagnoses have risen; they dispute the cause, not the fact.
explanations.E: Neither speaker disputes that clinicians treat such conditions.

difficultyReason: Arts-domain evaluative disagreement. Speakers make one explicit claim each about whether a museum should return a specific artifact. Direct contradiction; distractors are off-topic or agreed-upon.
stimulus: Curator Ambrose: Our museum should return the bronze statue to its country of origin. It was removed during a colonial expedition without the consent of the local community, and holding onto it today perpetuates that injustice. Director Basile: We should not return it. The statue has been carefully preserved and publicly displayed here for over a century, and returning it now would mean fewer people could see and study it. Our obligation is to public access.
questionStem: Ambrose and Basile disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the bronze statue was removed without local consent

choices.label: B
choices.text: the museum should return the bronze statue to its country of origin

choices.label: C
choices.text: the statue has been preserved at the museum

choices.label: D
choices.text: public access to artifacts is a consideration for museums

choices.label: E
choices.text: colonial-era acquisitions were sometimes carried out without consent

explanations.correct: Ambrose says the museum should return the statue; Basile says it should not. Direct contradiction of the central proposal.
explanations.A: Ambrose asserts this; Basile does not deny it.
explanations.C: Both accept the statue has been preserved at the museum.
explanations.D: Both treat public access as a legitimate consideration; they weigh it differently.
explanations.E: Both would accept this general point.

difficultyReason: Economics domain with a straightforward disagreement about whether raising tariffs will help domestic manufacturers. Direct contradiction; distractors are out-of-scope or agreement traps.
stimulus: Diego: Raising tariffs on imported steel will help our domestic steel manufacturers. With foreign steel made more expensive, buyers will turn to domestic mills, and our producers will gain customers and revenue. Elise: Raising tariffs will not help our domestic manufacturers. Most of them use imported steel as an input, and higher tariffs will raise their production costs enough to more than offset any gains from reduced foreign competition.

explanations.correct: Diego asserts the tariff will help domestic manufacturers; Elise explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction of the central claim.

explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the government's legal authority.
